newsitem.title: PERU: Deadline passes peacefully in Peru embassy seizure.
newsitem.headline: Deadline passes peacefully in Peru embassy seizure.

text.p: Leftist guerrillas holding at least 200 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Peru threatened to kill their captives on Wednesday, but a first deadline passed apparently without bloodshed.

The guerrillas issued an ultimatum at 11:15 a.m. (1615 GMT) giving President Alberto Fujimori an hour to negotiate before hostages would begin to be killed. They said Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela would be the first to die if up to 500 jailed comrades were not released.
However, no action appeared to have been taken by the time the deadline passed and rebel spokesmen asked for medicine to treat wounded from the original assault on the building.

Shortly before the morning ultimatum, an explosion and gunfire rocked the ambassador's residence in Lima where rebels from the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) stormed a reception on Tuesday night, taking hostages including senior diplomats and government ministers.
The rebels are demanding the release of 400 to 500 jailed comrades, including their leader Victor Polay, and safe passage to an Amazon jungle hideout.
It was unclear whether the blast before the ultimatum was caused by the guerrillas or by policemen surrounding the residence. There were no details of any injuries.
In Madrid, Spain's foreign ministry said there were wounded people inside the residence and rebels had asked Spain to mediate to get medical supplies in.

"They have asked Spain to ask Peru to allow medicines in for the wounded," the chief foreign ministry spokesman told Reuters. There was no immediate explanation of who was wounded or how serious their condition was.
The Polish foreign ministry also said the guerrillas had threatened to start shooting unless a doctor was sent to treat a wounded comrade.
The MRTA claimed they held 250 hostages after the release of about 80 women and old people early on Wednesday.

The stand-off followed a spectacular assault on Tuesday night during which heavily armed rebels attacked the ambassador's residence from outside while, according to some versions, guerrillas disguised as waiters joined in from the inside.

Juan Carlos Mejia, head of the special police task force handling the siege, confirmed the rebels had smuggled ammunition into the residence among flowers and Christmas cake. He could not, however, say whether some rebels had entered dressed as waiters.
Countries with nationals held in the siege appealed for calm in dealing with the crisis. Spain cautioned that the use of force could lead to a massacre.
Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar contacted President Fujimori and asked him to use psychological tactics to persuade the guerrillas to stand down.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said Germany had offered Peru help in resolving the crisis and he planned to appeal to Peruvian leaders to be prudent in their efforts to free the hostages.
Speaking to journalists in Bonn, Kinkel said he was trying to reach Fujimori by phone. Kinkel said he had been in contact with the foreign ministers of Japan and Austria.
Hostages included Foreign Minister Tudela, Agriculture Minister Rodolfo Munante Sanguineti, Supreme Court President Moises Pantoja and at least three local legislators.

Panama said 18 ambassadors were being held captive. Japan, Germany, Canada, Austria, Brazil, and Cuba were among countries to confirm the presence of their ambassadors. Other countries with diplomats held capitive included Poland, Spain, Cuba, Bolivia, Brazil, South Korea, France and Britain.

Washington condemned the "terrorist" attack, saying it hoped the siege would end quickly with the safe release of the hostages. The U.S. ambassador was not among those held but the State Department would not comment on other possible American captives.

Britain offered Peru its help in resolving the siege and said one member of Britain's embassy staff was among the hostages. "We stand ready to consider any request from the Peruvians for assistance," the foreign ministry said.
